section_summary: The section opens with U.S. responses to a Soviet complaint about a remark attributed to Prime Minister Yoshida, alongside reporting on Soviet criticism of Japan’s occupation and elections. Its largest group of documents concerns former agriculture minister Rikizō Hirano’s dismissal, his allegations of a political plot, and evidence about the wartime Kodokai. The final documents address the Katayama Cabinet’s resignation and the formation and reception of the Ashida Cabinet.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Soviet protest over Yoshida’s alleged remark
subfiles.about: Rejects the reported anti-Soviet remark attributed to Yoshida and cites Soviet criticism of the occupation.
subfiles.summary: The draft says investigators found no evidence Yoshida made the reported remark and attributes the sole American report to language difficulties. It says Japanese publication was barred under occupation rules, then quotes Soviet radio and newspaper attacks on the United States and the Yoshida Cabinet.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ambassador Novikov on Yoshida’s alleged remark
subfiles.about: Answers the Soviet complaint and asks that hostile Soviet media attacks cease.
subfiles.summary: The revised note denies evidence that Yoshida made the quoted remark and says it was never published in Japan. It supplies examples of Soviet broadcasts and newspapers attacking U.S. occupation policy, then asks Moscow to prevent recurrence.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Soviet chargé’s note
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Soviet complaint and requests MacArthur’s comments before a substantive reply.
subfiles.summary: The Department cannot confirm press accounts of Yoshida’s interview and promises a further answer after receiving information from Japan.

subfiles.title: Airgram forwarding translation of Soviet complaint
subfiles.to: U.S. Political Adviser to SCAP, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the Soviet note demanding action over Yoshida’s alleged anti-Soviet statement.
subfiles.summary: The translated note recounts newspaper reports of Yoshida favoring American protection after occupation, quotes his alleged reference to a dangerous northern enemy, and asks that he be called to account.

subfiles.title: Izvestiya analysis of Japanese parliamentary elections
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Soviet newspaper article criticizing occupation handling of Japan’s April elections.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reports Izvestiya claims that intimidation and occupation support sustained Yoshida’s weakened Liberals, while Socialists gained the most seats. It notes the article’s criticism of MacArthur’s description of Communist electoral losses.

subfiles.title: Forwarding Hirano’s statement on his dismissal
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, Acting Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits Hirano’s statement and seven supporting items while withholding judgment on its claims.
subfiles.summary: Sebald describes Hirano’s allegations as one-sided and says his mission lacks enough information to evaluate them.

subfiles.title: Hirano’s statement concerning his dismissal
subfiles.about: Argues that threats of prosecution and purge were used in a political plot to remove him from office.
subfiles.summary: Hirano recounts discussions with ministers, SCAP officials and journalists before Katayama dismissed him for alleged non-cooperation. He denies wrongdoing over his screening questionnaire and disputes reports of his views on rice prices, coal policy and the peace conference. He portrays Nishio’s alliances with left Socialists and Ashida’s Cabinet plans as motives for his removal, then requests formal confirmation that he is eligible for public office.

subfiles.title: Kodokai: purpose and difference from patriotic organizations
subfiles.doc_type: enclosed translated statement and evidence list
subfiles.about: Presents Kodokai as an anti-militarist organization and lists evidence supporting Hirano’s eligibility.
subfiles.summary: The statement says Kodokai used patriotic language as cover while opposing aggressive militarists and supporting General Ugaki. It lists publications, certificates, votes and records intended to show that wartime authorities monitored and dissolved the group.

subfiles.title: Ugaki certificate on the character of Kodokai
subfiles.about: Certifies that Kodokai and Hirano opposed aggressive militarism.
subfiles.summary: Ugaki describes his own reformist position, Hirano’s support for it, and military pressure on Kodokai. He says the organization backed his attempted Cabinet formation and later foreign policy, and was dissolved by the Tōjō Cabinet.

subfiles.title: Former gendarmerie officer’s certificate on Kodokai
subfiles.from: Former Tokyo gendarmerie officer, name unclear
subfiles.about: States that Kodokai stood outside nationalist organizations and faced possible dissolution.
subfiles.summary: The former officer describes Kodokai as linked to Ugaki’s anti-militarist group.

subfiles.title: Ainosuke Iwata certificate on Kodokai
subfiles.about: Confirms Kodokai did not join nationalist movements.
subfiles.summary: Iwata says nationalists regarded Kodokai and the agricultural union as socialist organizations.

subfiles.title: Yuji certificate on Kodokai
subfiles.about: Describes Kodokai as anti-militarist and outside nationalist movements.
subfiles.summary: The signer says Kodokai supported Ugaki’s pacifist group and was considered socialist.

subfiles.title: Kuniji Yamagata certificate on Kodo
subfiles.about: Explains Hirano’s nominal connection to Kodokai’s periodical Kodo.
subfiles.summary: Yamagata says Okuno edited Kodo and Hirano was only its nominal publisher.

subfiles.title: Japanese militarists and Kodokai
subfiles.about: Contrasts Japanese Army factions and places Kodokai with Ugaki’s anti-expansionist group.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on published accounts, the memorandum contrasts Tanaka’s expansionism with Ugaki’s stated preference for reform and international cooperation. It describes later rival Army factions and concludes that Kodokai supported neither, aligning instead with Ugaki.

subfiles.title: Sebald letter on Allied Council discussion of Katayama’s resignation
subfiles.about: Reports disagreement with MacArthur over a Soviet agenda item on the Japanese Cabinet change.
subfiles.summary: Sebald says MacArthur opposed having GHQ explain the Katayama Cabinet’s resignation before the Allied Council. Sebald permitted a reworded discussion item but anticipated a Soviet attempt to delay formation of a new Cabinet.

subfiles.title: Conversation with General Kislenko
subfiles.about: Records negotiations over an Allied Council agenda item concerning Katayama’s resignation.
subfiles.summary: Kislenko sought information from GHQ on the outgoing and prospective Cabinets. Sebald objected to wording that would compel a GHQ report and to discussion that might intrude on Japanese politics, but accepted a revised agenda title allowing Council members to discuss the matter.

subfiles.title: MacArthur statement on Katayama Cabinet resignation
subfiles.about: States that Japan’s Diet will resolve the Cabinet change through democratic procedure.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur praises Katayama’s Cabinet and leaves selection of its successor to Japanese representatives.

subfiles.title: Composition of the Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.about: Reports completion and membership of the Ashida coalition Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The airgram lists ministers and party affiliations following the Cabinet’s March 10 attestation.

subfiles.title: Chinese editorial on the Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.about: Reports a Chinese newspaper’s criticism of Japan’s new Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The editorial warns of conservative influence and doubts the coalition’s strength.

subfiles.title: Formation of the Ashida Cabinet
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Introduces a conversation with Matsumoto about selection of Ashida’s ministers.
subfiles.summary: The opening page reports Ashida’s advisers, candidate screening, coalition negotiations and Katayama’s refusal of the foreign affairs portfolio.
